title: Knowledge check: SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly covered in “SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics”?
options: SVG as an XML-based vector format
questions.answer_key: SVG as an XML-based vector format
questions.explanation: The attached XML curriculum lists “SVG as an XML-based vector format” under lesson 163, “SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics”. The other options are from different topics or unrelated areas.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the most reliable rule to remember when applying “SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics”?
options: Test valid and invalid samples, record the processor/version, and verify failure handling as well as success.
Test only one sample and infer all cases.
Publish generated output without validating it.
Assume pretty-printing preserves all whitespace semantics.
questions.answer_key: Test valid and invalid samples, record the processor/version, and verify failure handling as well as success.
questions.explanation: The correct choice separates the relevant XML concepts and avoids assumptions about processor behavior. Check the linked standard and actual implementation for details.

questions.prompt: After creating an example for “SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics”, what is the best next step?
options: Verify a normal case, an invalid or boundary case, and document the tool/version used.
Rely on visual appearance without parsing or validation.
Change several parts at once and infer the cause if the result changes.
questions.answer_key: Verify a normal case, an invalid or boundary case, and document the tool/version used.
questions.explanation: A small, reproducible test suite distinguishes expected behavior from a lucky example and makes version assumptions visible.
